questions.q: What two elements does Dicks say a good story must have?
a: A transformation and the teller as the protagonist
A surprising twist and a memorable villain
A clear moral and a happy ending
A timeline and several named characters
questions.why: Lesson 1 says stories need some kind of change and should be told by the person who lived them.

questions.q: What is the dinner test for a story?
a: Ask whether you would tell it to a friend over dinner
Try it on family before an audience
Keep it shorter than a dinner conversation
Ask a friend to rate it while you eat
questions.why: Lesson 2 says if you would not recount the story at dinner, you should not share it.

questions.q: What should you avoid doing when telling a story, according to lesson 2?
a: Acting out the drama with gestures and flowery language
Making eye contact with your listeners
Pausing before an important moment
Drawing on details from your own life
questions.why: Lesson 2 warns that theatrical gestures and poetic ornamentation distract from the message.

questions.q: Why do audiences respond better when the storyteller is the protagonist?
a: Personal vulnerability makes the story land with them
It keeps the story factually accurate
It spares listeners from judging other people
It makes the story shorter to tell
questions.why: Lesson 1 says sharing something personal takes courage and leaves a real mark on the audience.

questions.q: In the author's car crash story, which moment was the real five-second turning point?
a: His friends arriving to support him before surgery
The dashboard crushing his legs
His body flying through the windshield
His parents arriving at the hospital
questions.why: Lesson 3 says the crash itself was not the moment; the change came when friends showed up before surgery.
